papers.title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27500v1

summary.one_liner: Turnout is a post-hoc linearization method for a pretrained full-attention language model that keeps both attention paths and uses an RL-trained policy to decide per layer when to switch to a fixed-size linear path during long reasoning generations, trading memory use against answer correctness.
summary.plain: Language models normally store a growing memory of everything they have generated so far, which gets expensive when they write long chains of reasoning. This paper converts an existing model to use a fixed-size memory instead, which saves memory but usually makes answers less accurate. The authors keep the original path, add a trained shortcut path, and learn a rule that decides when each layer should switch between them, trained with a reward for both correct answers and low memory use.
summary.why:
Long reasoning tasks are costly for memory, so a method that reduces memory while limiting the accuracy loss could matter for deploying such models. The text reports that the learned switching policy gives a better accuracy-efficiency tradeoff than fixed switching and static hybrid baselines, but the text gives no further detail on size of gains, so its practical weight is unclear.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Transformer attention: the mechanism language models use to look back at earlier tokens.
- Key-value (KV) cache: the stored record of earlier tokens that grows as a response gets longer.
- Linear attention: a variant with a fixed-size state instead of a growing cache, cheaper in memory but often less accurate.
- Linearization / distillation: converting a trained model to the cheaper variant by training the new path to imitate the original.
- Hybrid model: a model that mixes full and linear attention layers.
- Reinforcement learning (RL) policy: a learned decision rule, here trained with a reward that balances correctness and memory use.
- Pareto frontier: the set of trade-offs where you cannot improve accuracy without spending more memory.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.

papers.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27973v1

summary.one_liner: MemOnce proposes a memory architecture for LLMs that stores a small set of final-layer hidden states as compact memory, decodes them back into KV caches on demand, and uses sparse retrieval with indices computed once across layers to cut memory growth and latency in long-context continual use.
summary.plain: Chatbots that talk with someone over a long time have to keep track of everything said so far, and the usual method stores a growing pile of working notes that eats up computer memory and slows responses. This paper proposes a design that keeps only a small, compressed set of summaries, rebuilds the detailed working notes from them only when needed, and pulls up just the relevant pieces. The authors report that adapting a 4-billion-parameter Qwen3.5 model this way cut the stored memory state by about 1313 times and prefill (the initial processing of input) latency by 6.9 times at a 1-million-token context.
summary.why: Memory cost is a main limit on running language models over very long or ongoing conversations, so a method that shrinks it while keeping detail could matter for practical deployment. The text is only an abstract, though, so the reported gains are the authors' own claims and have not been checked against independent tests or full experimental details.
summary.background:
- Transformer language models store a "KV cache": per-token attention keys and values for every layer, which grows with context length.
- Linear-time architectures compress history into a fixed-size state, which is cheaper but can lose fine detail.
- Hidden states are the internal numerical representations a model produces at each layer.
- Sparse attention means attending to only a selected subset of past items instead of all of them.
- Prefill latency is the delay before the model starts generating, while it processes the input.
- Context length (for example 1M tokens) is how much text the model can consider at once.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
